name: Shangaci / Shangaji = Enatthembo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Devos, Maud. 2013. Vowel length in Shangaci: when lexical vowel length and penultimate lengthening co-occur. Africana Linguistica 19: 85-107. doi:10.3406/aflin.2013.1018 (open access on Persée).
catalog_locator: sec. 2 pp. 86-87 (tone system, H retraction); sec. 3.1 pp. 88-89 (PUL and phonological phrasing; Downing/Hyman penult-stress remark); sec. 3.3 p. 93 (Portuguese loans); sec. 3.4 p. 94 + fn. 12
catalog_quote: [p.86] Shangaci is a tonal language with each mora being either high or low. Tone assignment rules and tonal processes can be described by referring exclusively to high tones. In nominal and verbal tonology, high tones are assigned on lexical and morphological grounds respectively. [p.87] High tone retraction is applied to a high tone assigned to the last vowel of a phonological phrase. As will be discussed below, the penultimate vowel of a phonological phrase is automatically lengthened. If the following ultimate vowel has a high tone assigned to it, it retracts to the second mora of the lengthened penultimate vowel. [p.88, 3.1] Words that are uttered in isolation always have penultimate lengthening (PUL) applied to them. Within a sentence PUL marks the end of a phonological phrase. [p.89] As shown in Downing (2004: 122) and Hyman (2009) penult stress is a widespread phenomenon in Bantu languages and its most common phonetic correlate is vowel lengthening. ... The fact that Shangaci has PUL, although neighbouring Makhuwa variants as well as Koti lack it, need therefore not come as a surprise.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the text we hold layer of Devos 2013, from the Persée PDF alongside it). All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators (the [..] marks genuine omissions): p.86 sec. 2 'Shangaci is a tonal language with each mora being either high or low. Tone assignment rules.. In nominal and verbal tonology, high tones are assigned on lexical and morphological grounds respectively.'; p.88 sec. 3.1 'Words that are uttered in isolation always have penultimate lengthening (PUL) applied to them. Within a sentence PUL marks the end of a phonological phrase.'; p.89 'As shown in Downing (2004: 122) and Hyman (2009) penult stress is a widespread phenomenon in Bantu languages and its…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shangaci is a tone language (lexical H in nouns, morphologically assigned H in verbs, with H doubling and retraction); it has no lexical stress, but the penultimate syllable of every phonological phrase (hence of every word in isolation/citation form) is automatically lengthened, which the author identifies with Bantu penult stress; a phrase-final H retracts onto the lengthened penult.
new_statements.exceptions: PUL does not apply phrase-medially (e.g. noun + possessive phrase together, so the noun's penult is not lengthened); PUL neutralises lexical vowel length in phrase-final penults; Portuguese loans show long vowels where Portuguese had stress; neighbouring Makhuwa varieties and Koti lack PUL.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological phrase, not the word: penult lengthening marks the right edge of the phonological phrase; citation forms (words in isolation) always show it. Author notes (fn. 12) that no controlled acoustic study has been done.
new_statements.identity_note: Devos's 'Shangaci' (2008-2014 spelling) / 'Shangaji' (2016- spelling) is the language Glottolog files as Nathembo [nath1238], ISO 639-3 nte (Ethnologue name Nathembo; autonym Esakaji/Sakati); Glottolog itself attaches Devos's Shangaci publications to nath1238. Described variety: the coastal village north of Angoche, Nampula province; a Makhuwa (P30) x Swahili contact language closely related to Koti [koti1238]. No dialect differentiation is discussed.

sources.note: Sec. 2 (p.86): Shangaci is a tonal language, each mora H or L; H tones lexical in nouns, morphologically assigned in verbs, with H doubling and retraction. Sec. 3/3.1 (p.88): automatic penultimate lengthening (PUL) at the end of a phonological phrase; words in isolation always have PUL. p.89: PUL is treated as the Shangaci reflex of Bantu penult stress (Downing 2004, Hyman 2009), notable because neighbouring Makhuwa and Koti lack it. p.93: stressed syllables of Portuguese loans surface as long vowels. p.94: PUL neutralises lexical length in phrase-final penults.

sources.quote: There are also prosodic traces of the augment: the tonal pattern of Shangaji nouns is probably the result of the H tone of a former augment and/or a lexical H tone (cf. van der Wal 2006 for a similar analysis of Makhuwa nominal tone). [fn. 15, p. 313] || Shangaji has automatic penultimate lengthening (PUL) at the end of a phonological phrase. Nouns uttered in isolation have PUL applied to them. [fn. 1, p. 290] || There is a prosodic difference between the nominal prefixes 2 and 2a. The a- prefix of class 2a is extra-prosodic, i.e., it does not count as part of the noun for tone assignment. The segmentally identical a- prefix of class 2 does count as part of the noun for tone assignment. [fn. 5, p. 291] || There is no audible difference between mphu'la 'in the nose' and mphu'la 'nose'. Both share the same tonal pattern and begin with a homorganic syllabic nasal. [...] As connectives are prosodically part of the following noun, they cause tonal changes, which, however, are blocked by locative nominal prefixes. [fn. 16, p. 314]
